Introduction
Medical databases are continuously updated and iterated,
with the number of observed values and the variety of
variables constantly increasing, leading to increasingly rich
data content. This results in a significant increase in the size
of individual data files, including both an increase in the
number of rows (length) and an expansion in the number
of columns (width) [1]. For example, in the MIMIC 3.0
database, the number of records in the chartevents file has
reached the hundred‐million level [2]; the numeric file in
the Amsterdam Critical Care Database version 1.0.2 is
similarly large [3].
Despite their massive number of records, these files have
relatively simple variable structures. For example, the charte-
vents file primarily contains fields such as patient ID, item, and
value. In contrast, some other databases, though having fewer
observations, feature a large number of variables. For example,
the core file in the first wave (Wave 1) of the ELSA data set
contains only 12,099 records but includes as many as 4484
variables [4].
Such a large‐scale database faces numerous challenges dur-
ing querying, cleaning, and processing. Currently, common
data access methods include SQL queries, distributed storage
system conversion, and specialized data platforms. SQL
queries, as the standard method, are versatile but require
users to master the SQL language, have a steep learning
curve, and suffer from low efficiency for complex queries [5].
Distributed storage systems (e.g., Hadoop) offer strong scal-
ability but come with high deployment and maintenance
costs, requiring specialized technical teams, making them
unsuitable for most clinical researchers [6, 7]. As a result,
ordinary researchers often struggle to independently apply
such systems for analysis. To address these challenges, this
paper proposes an innovative data processing strategy based
on “slicing + dictionary” to enable flexible querying and
efficient extraction of medical big data, thereby enhancing
data accessibility and practicality.
2
|
Methods
2.1
|
Theoretical Basis of the Slicing + Dictionary
Method
The “slicing + dictionary” method is based on the theory
of data decomposition and restructuring, and has been
extended
and
applied
to
specific
application
scenarios
in medical big data. This method has the following theoret-
ical advantages: (1) It effectively reduces the amount of
data processed in a single operation, thereby significantly
reducing the consumption of computing resources; (2) It
constructs an efficient indexing system through preproces-
sing, enabling rapid data location and extraction, and
significantly improving query efficiency; (3) It maintains
clinical
relevance
during
data
decomposition
and
reorganization, ensuring the scientific validity and effec-
tiveness of the analysis results.

2.2
|
Technical Implementation
This method consists of two core components: data slicing and
dictionary construction.
2.2.1
|
Data Slicing
This study designed a multi‐dimensional data slicing strategy to
adapt to the needs of different clinical studies. Specifically, it
includes: Clinical Dimension Slicing: Data is divided according to
parameter types (such as vital signs, laboratory tests, drug use,
etc.); Event Dimension Slicing: Data views are constructed around
key clinical events (such as intubation, medication, surgery, etc.);
Hybrid Dimension Slicing: Composite slices are created by
combining multiple features to meet complex analysis needs.
The slicing granularity can be flexibly adjusted according to data
characteristics and application scenarios to achieve a balance
between query performance and storage efficiency. Inspired by
distributed database sharding technology, this design introduces
clinical semantic considerations to make data slicing more in line
with medical research thinking patterns [8, 9]. For example, the
chartevents table in the MIMIC database can be sliced according
to different clinical measurement items (such as blood pressure,
blood oxygen saturation, body temperature, etc.), or drug‐related
data can be sliced according to drug names. The slicing process
supports multi‐level granularity, allowing researchers to flexibly
adjust the level of detail of the slicing according to actual needs.
2.2.2
|
Dictionary Construction
The dictionary system serves as a bridge connecting user query
intentions with data slices, featuring the following key elements:
Encoding‐Description‐Location‐Attribute Structure: Each dictio-
nary entry includes standard encoding, clinical description, data
location, and attribute information; Multi‐level Classification Sys-
tem: Construct a hierarchical dictionary system based on clinical
domains, parameter types, measurement methods, etc.; Synonym
Mapping: enabling unified retrieval of terms from different ter-
minology systems and expressions; Cross‐database compatibility
design: enabling mapping and connectivity between different
databases for the same clinical concepts. This dictionary system
draws on the experience of the Unified Medical Language System
in integrating biomedical terminology, adopting a multi‐level
structure of encoding‐description‐location‐attributes to achieve
semantic mapping between clinical concepts and data locations
[10]. By integrating multidimensional information such as clinical
terms, parameter types, and measurement methods, and estab-
lishing cross‐database term mapping relationships, researchers can
retrieve and analyze data using standardized clinical terms [11,
12]. The aim is to establish a semantic bridge between clinical
concepts and data locations, enabling researchers to directly
retrieve and analyze data using familiar clinical terms (rather than
database field names).
Through
dictionary
indexing,
researchers
can
precisely
locate and extract the required specific data subsets, avoiding
unnecessary processing of the entire data set, thereby signifi-
cantly improving the efficiency of retrieval and analysis.
2.3
|
Slicing Classification
Based on the direction of data segmentation, slices can be cat-
egorized into vertical slices and horizontal slices, also known as
row slices and column slices, or observation slices and variable
slices.
In scenarios where the volume of data is dominated by the
number of rows, that is, typical long‐format data, the number of
records continues to increase with database version updates,
while the number of variables remains largely unchanged. In
such cases, using vertical slicing (row slicing/observation slic-
ing) is more appropriate. For example, in the MIMIC database's
chartevents file, the number of records expands over time, but
the field structure remains largely fixed.
Conversely, when the data volume is primarily influenced by the
expansion of the number of columns, i.e., when the number of
variables is large and the number of records changes little, hori-
zontal slicing (column slicing/variable slicing) is more suitable.
For example, in certain social medicine surveys (such as ELSA),
although the sample size is limited, the data set becomes ex-
tremely large due to the extremely high number of variables.
In extremely large datasets where both the number of rows and
columns influence the data set size, both longitudinal slicing and
horizontal slicing strategies can be employed simultaneously to
achieve more flexible and efficient storage and querying.
3
|
Discussion
The core advantages of the slicing and dictionary method lie in:
reduced resource requirements (by loading slices on demand,
enabling ordinary computing devices to process large‐scale
data), improved query efficiency (accurately locating the
required data, avoiding full table scans, and significantly
improving query speed), enhanced flexibility (supporting multi‐
dimensional slicing and customizable dictionaries to adapt to
diverse research needs), and cross‐database universality (the
method design does not depend on specific database structures).
These advantages directly address the limitations of traditional
analysis methods in medical big data analysis proposed by
Binder and Blettner, and as validated by Chrimes and Zamani,
appropriate data structure design can effectively solve the core
issues of medical data integration and querying [7, 13].
4
|
Limitations and Challenges
This method also faces several limitations: slice design trade‐
offs (slice granularity must balance access efficiency and storage
redundancy), update and maintenance costs (database updates
require synchronized updates to slices and dictionaries), sup-
port for non‐standard queries (extremely specialized queries
may require custom slice strategies), and initial setup effort
(initial implementation requires significant effort for slice and
dictionary construction). Dinov points out that the processing
and analysis of large‐scale medical data are characterized by
high costs and high complexity. Khan et al. emphasize that the
technical challenges of big data processing primarily lie in rapid

challenges are also present in the slicing dictionary method and
must be fully considered during implementation. This initial
investment may be offset by long‐term efficiency improvements
and enhanced accessibility, particularly for institutions con-
ducting multiple studies [14, 15].
5
|
Future Outlook
Future research will focus on: automated slicing optimization
(developing intelligent algorithms to automatically determine the
optimal slicing strategy), dictionary self‐learning (continuously
optimizing dictionary structure based on user query patterns),
cloud‐based deployment models (researching cloud‐based slicing
dictionary services to further lower the usage threshold), and
integration with AI/ML workflows (optimizing the integration of
slicing dictionary methods with machine learning workflows).
With the advancement of natural language processing and
machine learning technologies, slicing dictionary methods are
expected to further enhance their intelligence and usability.
6
|
Conclusion
Slicing
and
dictionary
methods
offer
a
new
paradigm
for addressing the challenges of accessing large‐scale medical
databases. By partitioning large data files according to clinical
dimensions and establishing standardized dictionary mappings,
this method has the potential to significantly reduce technical
barriers and resource requirements while improving query
efficiency and flexibility. The theoretical foundation of this
method aligns with existing research findings, indicating that it
could enable ordinary clinical researchers to efficiently access
and analyze large‐scale medical data that was previously difficult
to handle, thereby providing an important tool for advancing
medical research and evidence‐based medical practice.
In the future, this method is expected to be extended to broader
medical data domains, promoting the democratization and
value extraction of medical big data, and ultimately accelerating
the transformation from data to knowledge, improving patient
outcomes, and optimizing the allocation of medical resources.
Future work will focus on the practical implementation and
performance validation of the method, as well as its optimiza-
tion and adaptation for different clinical research scenarios.
